title: Succession Looks Different When the Business Belongs to a Community, Not One Founder
excerpt: For Indigenous-owned enterprises and social enterprises, succession rarely means a trade sale. It means governance, relationships and a valuation question most founders have never had to answer.
content:
Most succession conversations start from the same assumption: one founder, one business, and eventually a trade sale or a handover to a family member who has been groomed for the role. For Indigenous-owned enterprises and social enterprises across Queensland, NSW and Victoria, that assumption rarely holds. Ownership often sits with a community, a trust, or a board representing several family groups, built deliberately to protect intergenerational or community benefit rather than concentrate it in one person's hands.

That structure is the whole point of these organisations, and it is not a problem to be solved. But it does mean succession is a genuinely different planning exercise, not a smaller or simpler version of the standard SME playbook. Many of these businesses have also grown quickly in recent years through government and corporate procurement relationships that specifically seek out Indigenous-owned suppliers, which means the succession question is often arriving earlier in the organisation's life than a founder expects, well before anyone has had the chance to think it through properly.

The pattern we see across mission-driven organisations is not that leadership has avoided the topic. It is that the standard framing, who do I sell to and what do I get for it, simply does not map onto a structure where ownership was never designed to transfer that way in the first place. The planning problem is real. It just needs a different shape.

Why the Usual Succession Playbook Doesn't Fit

A typical SME succession plan separates into one track: the founder identifies a successor, decision rights transfer gradually, and the business is eventually sold or handed over at an agreed value. Inside a community or trust-owned enterprise, that single track usually needs to split into two. Operational succession, who runs the organisation day to day, answers the phone, manages the team and delivers the work, can move on a relatively normal timeline. Governance succession, who sits on the board or council, who holds signing authority, and who the organisation's major funders and corporate partners actually deal with, often runs on a completely different clock, set by community process rather than a single person's retirement date.

Treating these as one decision is where the planning usually stalls. A founder who is ready to step back operationally may still be, in practice, the only person the board, the bank and the major contract holders actually recognise. Separating the two tracks early is what makes either one possible to plan properly.

Where the Relationship Risk Actually Sits

In a conventional business sale, buyers price in owner dependency, the risk that key client relationships, decisions and institutional knowledge sit with one person rather than the organisation. The same pattern shows up here, just without a buyer to price it. Funders, corporate partners who hold Indigenous procurement targets, and the trust the broader community places in the organisation are frequently relationships the founding leader built personally over many years. None of that transfers automatically just because a new name appears on a letterhead.

This is worth taking as seriously as a lender or an investor would. The thinking behind an exit readiness assessment, mapping exactly which relationships, contracts and decisions still depend on one individual, applies just as usefully to a governance transition with no sale attached as it does to a business heading toward one.

What 'Worth' Means When There's No Trade Sale Coming

Most of these organisations are not heading toward a trade sale, and that can make valuation feel beside the point. It usually isn't. A board still needs a defensible view of what the organisation is worth to make sound decisions about reinvestment, insurance, debt capacity, and any buyout owed to a departing leader who holds a personal equity stake inside a broader trust or corporate structure. Those decisions get made with far more confidence when they rest on an actual number rather than a guess carried in one person's head.

An indicative business valuation gives a board that number without assuming a sale is coming, along with a clear read on which parts of the organisation are genuinely driving that value and which are propped up by relationships that have not yet been documented or shared beyond the founder.

Starting the Conversation While the Founder Is Still in the Room

The organisations that handle this well are not the ones with the cleanest paperwork. They are the ones that start the governance succession conversation years before the founder actually intends to step back, while that person is still available to introduce the next leader to funders personally, hand over signing authority gradually, and sit in meetings as a mentor rather than the only person who can answer the question. That window closes faster than most boards expect, and it cannot be recovered once the founder has genuinely moved on.

None of this is a criticism of how these organisations are run. Dual mission structures are built to protect something more durable than a single owner's exit, and that is precisely why the succession plan needs to be built with the same deliberateness as the mission itself. A fractional CFO partnership gives a board or council an outside financial partner through that transition, someone who can hold the valuation, the reporting and the funder relationships in view while governance finds its footing. If that transition is somewhere on your organisation's horizon, it is worth starting the conversation sooner than feels urgent.

faqs.q: How is succession different for an Indigenous-owned enterprise or social enterprise?
faqs.a: Succession usually splits into two separate tracks rather than one. Operational succession covers who runs the organisation day to day, while governance succession covers who sits on the board, holds signing authority, and manages relationships with funders and corporate partners. These two tracks often run on different timelines, set by community process rather than a single founder's retirement date.

faqs.q: What does exit readiness mean for an organisation with no planned sale?
faqs.a: Exit readiness in this context is less about preparing for a buyer and more about mapping which relationships, contracts and decisions still depend on one individual. An exit readiness style assessment surfaces that dependency clearly, which is exactly the information a board needs before a founder steps back from governance.

faqs.q: Can a community-owned or trust-owned business still get a formal valuation?
faqs.a: Yes. A valuation does not require a sale to be useful. Boards use an indicative business valuation to make informed decisions about reinvestment, debt capacity, insurance, and any buyout owed to a leader who holds personal equity within a broader trust or corporate structure. It gives the board a defensible number to plan from rather than a figure carried in one person's head.

faqs.q: Who should hold signing authority if a founding director steps back?
faqs.a: This is a governance decision for the board or council, not just an operational one, and it works best when it is resolved gradually rather than all at once. The founder introducing the incoming signatory to funders, lenders and major contract holders personally, before stepping back fully, protects relationships that would otherwise need to be rebuilt from scratch.

faqs.q: Can a fractional CFO support succession planning in a mission-driven organisation?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly where a board is managing a leadership transition alongside funding cycles and commercial reporting. A fractional CFO partnership gives a board an outside financial partner who can hold the valuation, reporting and funder relationships steady while governance succession plays out, rather than leaving that continuity resting on one departing leader.

faqs.q: When should an Indigenous-owned enterprise start planning for leadership transition?
faqs.a: Earlier than feels urgent. The organisations that manage this well start years before the founder intends to step back, while that person is still available to introduce the next leader to funders and partners personally and hand over signing authority gradually, rather than leaving governance to catch up after the fact.

faqs.q: Why do funding and corporate partners sometimes hesitate after a leadership change?
faqs.a: Many funders and corporate partners build their relationship with a specific person rather than the organisation as an entity, especially where that person has represented the business personally for years. That trust has to be actively transferred through direct introductions and shared decision-making, it rarely moves automatically just because a new title appears on a letterhead.
